articles.body_html:
I’ve been looking at how developers can bring AI coding agents into their existing workflows, and Jira is an interesting place to start. Many engineering teams already use it to manage bugs, feature requests, sprints, and backlogs. The problem is that having a ticket in Jira does not automatically mean an AI coding agent can pick it up, work on the code, and return the results for review.

At the same time, Atlassian is bringing more AI capabilities into its products through Rovo. These features are useful, but teams that want to use their own coding agents may not want to depend on another AI usage allowance just to connect their existing development workflow.

So I wanted to explore a practical alternative: using Jira with your own AI coding agents without paying for additional Rovo credits.

The idea is straightforward. Keep Jira as your issue tracker, connect it to a tool that coordinates agent execution, and let agents such as Claude Code or Codex work on assigned tasks using the subscriptions or API accounts you already have.

One option for doing this is Sharkly. It connects Jira issues to agent-driven development tasks, lets teams assign work to their existing coding agents, and provides a place to track execution and review results.

In this guide, I’ll walk through how the workflow works, how to set it up, what you can do with it, and what “free” actually means.

Why Use AI Agents with Jira?

Jira is good at organizing work. You can create issues, assign responsibilities, prioritize bugs, plan sprints, and track progress.

But there is still a gap between managing a task and completing it.

Imagine a Jira ticket that says:

Fix the validation error that occurs when users submit the registration form with an invalid email address. Add tests to cover the affected cases.

A developer would normally open the repository, investigate the issue, make the change, run tests, and submit a pull request. They would then update Jira so the rest of the team knows what happened.

An AI coding agent can help with much of that implementation work. It can inspect the code, propose a fix, modify files, run tests, and potentially create a pull request.

The challenge is connecting those steps to the existing Jira workflow.

Without an integration, someone may have to copy the ticket description into an AI tool, manually provide repository context, monitor the run, and paste the results back into Jira.

That works for occasional tasks, but it becomes tedious when a team has dozens of tickets.

Connecting Jira to an agent execution workflow can help teams:

  • Assign coding tasks to AI agents from existing engineering work.
  • Preserve ticket descriptions and acceptance criteria.
  • Reduce manual copying between Jira and coding tools.
  • Track execution, blockers, and results.
  • Run independent tasks in isolated workspaces.
  • Review AI-generated changes before merging them.

The goal is not to remove developers from the process. It is to reduce the repetitive work between identifying a problem and producing a reviewable solution.

Do You Need to Pay for Rovo Credits to Use AI Agents with Jira?

Not necessarily. It depends on which AI capabilities and integrations you use.

Atlassian's Rovo provides AI-powered search, chat, agents, and other capabilities across supported Atlassian products. Rovo usage is measured through credits for certain AI interactions and enriched Teamwork Graph API calls. The included allowance depends on your Atlassian plan and eligible products. See Atlassian's Rovo pricing and usage information.

However, Jira does not require every external coding agent to use Rovo for its code execution.

You can connect Jira to a separate workflow tool and use a coding agent that runs through your own existing subscription or API account. In that setup, the coding agent's model usage is handled by the agent provider rather than being automatically charged as Rovo usage.

For example, Sharkly offers a Jira integration and supports coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex. Its published pricing says the product is free for teams of up to 10 people, while model usage stays on the coding plans and API accounts the team already uses. Check the Sharkly website for current plan details.

Here is the important distinction:

So when I say you can use Jira with AI agents for free, I mean you can avoid paying for an additional Rovo-based coding workflow by using your existing agent setup and a free coordination plan where eligible.

It does not mean that every component of the workflow is free. Your Jira subscription, coding-agent plan, API consumption, and infrastructure can still have costs.

What You Need Before Getting Started

Before setting up the integration, make sure you have the following:

  • A Jira account with access to the project you want to use.
  • A Sharkly account.
  • A coding agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, configured on a computer.
  • Access to the repository where the agent will work.
  • Permission to connect the Jira project, or help from a Jira administrator if required.

You do not need to migrate your entire Jira backlog to get started. You can connect a single project and try the workflow on a low-risk task first.

Step 1: Set Up Your AI Coding Agent

Start with the coding agent you already use rather than choosing a new model just for the Jira integration.

For example, you might already have Claude Code or Codex configured on your development machine. Make sure it can access the intended repository and that its authentication is working.

You should also verify that the agent can perform the basic actions required for your task, such as:

  • Reading relevant source files.
  • Editing code in the assigned workspace.
  • Running the project's tests.
  • Reporting errors or blockers.
  • Producing a reviewable change.

This matters because Sharkly coordinates work; the connected coding agent is still responsible for performing the coding.

If you have not configured an agent before, start with its official documentation:

  • Claude Code
  • OpenAI Codex

Use the provider account or API credentials you are authorized to use. You do not need to switch to a new model provider simply to connect Jira to Sharkly.

Step 2: Create Your Sharkly Workspace

Next, open Sharkly and set up your workspace.

Sharkly provides a shared environment for organizing tasks, assigning agents, tracking execution, and reviewing results. It is designed to work alongside existing development tools rather than replacing the coding agent itself.

Once your workspace is ready, connect a computer that has access to the repository and the coding-agent runtime you configured in Step 1.

A computer here is the execution environment where the agent actually runs. Depending on your setup, this can be your own development machine or another supported computer.

Before moving on, confirm that the computer is available and the intended coding-agent runtime is configured correctly.

Step 3: Connect Jira to Sharkly

Now connect your Jira project.

According to the Sharkly Jira integration documentation, the connection supports Jira Cloud as well as Jira Server and Data Center.

For Jira Cloud, you generally need:

  • Your Jira host, such as your-company.atlassian.net.
  • The email address of your Jira account.
  • An Atlassian API token.

For Jira Server or Data Center, the connection uses the Jira base URL, username, and a supported authentication method.

In Sharkly, open the integrations settings, select Jira, and choose the option to connect your Jira account. Enter the required details and follow the validation steps.

Keep API tokens private. Use an account with access to the project you want to connect, and follow your organization's credential-management policies.

Connecting the account does not automatically import or synchronize all your Jira data. You must choose how you want the project and its tasks to be connected.

Step 4: Link a Jira Project to a Sharkly Space

After connecting Jira, create a sync link between the Jira project and a Sharkly Space.

A Space is where the corresponding tasks and agent work are organized.

The setup process lets you select the Jira project, choose the target Space, configure synchronization, and review status and user mappings.

You generally have two approaches:

Option A: Synchronize a project

Use synchronization if you want Jira and Sharkly to remain connected as work progresses. Depending on the configured sync direction, supported changes to linked issues and tasks can flow between the two systems.

Option B: Import existing issues

Use import if you want to copy historical Jira issues into Sharkly, such as when testing a workflow or planning a migration.

You can also import existing work and enable ongoing synchronization as part of the setup.

For a team that wants to keep using Jira, I would start with a single project and a synchronization link. This allows the team to test agent execution without moving the entire backlog.

Review the issue status mappings and user mappings before confirming the connection. If your setup requires webhook permissions that your Jira account does not have, a Jira administrator may need to configure the webhook.

The official setup instructions are available here: Sharkly Jira integration.

Step 5: Choose a Jira Ticket for Your First Agent Task

Once the project is connected, select a small, well-defined issue.

I would avoid starting with a vague task such as “Improve the application” or a change that could affect production security, payment processing, or critical infrastructure.

Instead, choose something like:

  • Add validation for a missing field.
  • Fix a reproducible UI bug.
  • Add unit tests for an existing function.
  • Update an isolated component.
  • Investigate the cause of a failing test.

The quality of the ticket matters. An AI agent needs enough information to understand what success looks like.

For example, a useful ticket could read:

Title: Add validation for invalid email addresses

Description: The registration form currently accepts malformed email addresses. Add validation to reject invalid formats and display a clear error message.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Invalid email formats are rejected.
  • Valid email addresses continue to work.
  • The error message is understandable.
  • Tests cover valid and invalid inputs.
  • Existing registration behavior is not unintentionally changed.

The clearer the acceptance criteria, the easier it is to review the agent's result.

Step 6: Assign the Ticket to Your AI Agent

With the Jira project connected, its linked issue can appear as a task in Sharkly.

You can then assign that task to a configured agent, much as you would assign work to a teammate.

The agent configuration determines how the task is executed, including its instructions, runtime, and available resources.

For example, you might assign the registration-validation task to an agent configured to use Claude Code. The agent can inspect the relevant repository, implement the change, run tests, and report what it completed.

The same general approach can be used with other supported coding-agent runtimes.

The important thing is that the agent receives the actual task context instead of relying on someone to manually copy the ticket into a separate conversation.

If this is your first run, keep the scope small and make sure the agent has access only to the resources it needs.

Step 7: Let the Agent Work in an Isolated Environment

Once the task is assigned and the execution environment is ready, the agent can begin working.

Sharkly supports isolated workspaces for repository-backed tasks, including Git worktree-based execution. This helps separate concurrent coding tasks so they do not directly overwrite one another's working files.

That matters when you eventually want to run more than one agent at a time.

Imagine assigning three independent tickets:

  • Agent A adds a validation rule.
  • Agent B fixes a layout issue.
  • Agent C adds unit tests for a separate service.

If every agent edits the same working directory, changes can interfere with each other. Separate worktrees reduce that risk by keeping each task's changes isolated.

Isolation does not eliminate every integration problem. Two agents can still produce changes that conflict when branches are combined, so testing and review remain necessary.

During execution, use the task record to follow the agent's progress, inspect relevant output, and identify blockers.

Step 8: Review the Results and Pull Request

When the agent finishes, inspect its output before accepting the change.

Depending on the task and configured workflow, the agent may report its results, describe the files it changed, run tests, or create a pull request.

If you use Sharkly's GitHub integration, a pull request can be linked to the corresponding task through its task ID in the branch name, title, or body.

This helps connect the coding result back to the work item that initiated it.

Before approving anything, I would check:

  1. Did the agent address the actual requirements in the Jira ticket?
  2. Are the code changes limited to the intended scope?
  3. Did the relevant tests run, and did they pass?
  4. Are there any unexpected changes or dependencies?
  5. Does the implementation introduce security, performance, or compatibility concerns?

Do not treat an agent's claim that tests passed as a substitute for verifying the results when the change matters.

A pull request should still go through the team's normal review process. The agent can produce a proposed implementation, but a person should remain responsible for deciding whether the code is ready to merge and release.

Step 9: Keep Jira as the Source of Work

One of the main benefits of this workflow is that your team does not have to abandon Jira.

Product managers can continue writing requirements. Engineers can prioritize bugs and plan sprints. QA can follow issues through testing. AI agents can help implement selected tasks, while the team retains visibility into the work.

With a configured synchronization link, supported changes can flow between Jira and Sharkly. This reduces the need to maintain two completely separate records of the same task.

It is still worth defining how your team handles statuses, pull-request reviews, and final acceptance. For example, merging a pull request should not be assumed to close a Jira issue automatically unless you have explicitly configured the relevant workflow.

The aim is to make agent execution part of your existing process rather than introducing another disconnected place where work happens.

What Can You Automate Once the Integration Works?

After the first task succeeds, you can gradually expand the workflow.

Bug fixes

Assign agents reproducible bugs with clear acceptance criteria. Ask them to investigate the cause, implement a fix, and add tests.

Test generation

Use agents to add unit tests around existing functionality or cover specific edge cases. Review the tests to ensure they actually verify the expected behavior.

Small feature implementations

For well-scoped features, an agent can inspect the relevant code, implement the change, and return a pull request for review.

Technical investigations

An agent can inspect a codebase, trace a failure, identify likely causes, and document its findings. This can be useful even when you do not want it to modify the code.

Parallel engineering tasks

Once your team is comfortable with isolated execution, you can assign independent tickets to different agents. Start with tasks that do not depend on one another and increase concurrency gradually.

Not every task should be automated. Architecture decisions, ambiguous requirements, sensitive changes, and production releases may still need substantial human involvement.

How Much Can You Actually Save?

The main potential saving is not necessarily the cost of the model. It is the time spent moving between tools and coordinating work manually.

Consider a developer who spends time copying ticket descriptions, opening coding sessions, setting up branches, monitoring execution, and updating Jira after every task.

A connected workflow can reduce some of those repetitive steps.

The exact savings depend on the team's ticket volume, agent reliability, review requirements, and existing process. It would be misleading to promise a fixed productivity improvement without measuring your own workflow.

To evaluate whether the setup is worthwhile, start by tracking:

  • Time from ticket assignment to a reviewable change.
  • How much manual setup each task requires.
  • The proportion of agent tasks that produce usable results.
  • Time spent reviewing and correcting agent-generated changes.
  • The number of defects or rework items introduced.

If those metrics improve without compromising quality, the integration is doing its job.

Is This Better Than Using Rovo Directly?

That depends on what you want the agent to do.

Rovo provides AI capabilities within Atlassian's ecosystem, including search, chat, and agent functionality. It can be a natural choice if you want AI features that work directly with Atlassian's connected knowledge and applications.

A separate coding-agent workflow is useful when you want to use tools you already have, such as Claude Code or Codex, to work on a repository.

Here is how I would think about the distinction:

These approaches are not necessarily mutually exclusive. A team can use Rovo for some Atlassian-native tasks and external coding agents for repository work.

One thing to watch: Atlassian documents that certain enriched Teamwork Graph calls made through external tools, including its MCP server, consume Rovo credits. If you want to avoid additional Rovo usage, check whether your chosen workflow invokes those credit-consuming services. A standard Jira synchronization workflow and a workflow that requests enriched Rovo context are not the same thing.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Giving an agent a vague ticket

A vague issue often produces a vague implementation. Write acceptance criteria and define the expected result before assigning the work.

Starting with a high-risk task

Test the integration on a small, reversible change first. Confirm that repository access, tests, and review work as expected.

Giving the agent excessive permissions

Use a dedicated development environment where possible, and avoid exposing production credentials or unnecessary access.

Assuming synchronization means everything is automatic

Connecting Jira does not automatically import all historical data or guarantee that every event and status transition behaves exactly as your team expects. Review the synchronization settings and test them.

Treating generated code as production-ready

Agents can make mistakes, misunderstand requirements, or introduce regressions. Keep code review, testing, and release decisions in the hands of responsible team members.

Confusing free coordination with free model usage

A free platform plan does not necessarily include the cost of an AI model. Check which subscriptions, API keys, infrastructure, and usage limits apply to your setup.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use AI coding agents with Jira without paying for Rovo credits?

Yes, you can use an external coding-agent workflow connected to Jira without necessarily invoking Rovo's credit-consuming AI features. For example, Sharkly can connect Jira tasks to supported coding agents that use your existing subscriptions or API accounts. Avoiding Rovo credits depends on the integrations and features you actually use.

Is Sharkly free to use with Jira?

Sharkly's published pricing says it is free for teams of up to 10 people. Model usage remains with the coding plans or API accounts configured for your agents. Check Sharkly's website for the latest pricing and terms.

Do I have to move my tickets out of Jira?

No. You can connect a Jira project to a Sharkly Space and configure synchronization. You can import historical issues if needed, but you do not have to migrate your entire backlog just to try the workflow.

Which AI agents can I use?

Sharkly supports multiple coding-agent runtimes, including Claude Code and Codex, alongside other supported environments. Confirm that the runtime you want to use is supported and configured on your connected computer.

Can AI agents create pull requests from Jira tickets?

An agent can implement a task and create a pull request when its runtime, repository access, and workflow are configured to support that action. With Sharkly's GitHub integration, pull requests can be linked back to their tasks. The result should still be reviewed by a person.

Can multiple agents work on Jira tickets at the same time?

Yes, with an appropriate setup. Assigning independent tasks to different agents and running them in isolated workspaces can reduce interference. You should still account for compute limits, agent usage, dependencies between tickets, and the review workload.

Final Thoughts

I think one of the most useful ways to bring AI into software development is to start with the workflow a team already uses.

If your team manages its work in Jira, you do not necessarily need to replace that system or pay for another AI usage model just to start experimenting with coding agents.

By connecting Jira to a tool such as Sharkly, you can assign selected issues to existing coding agents, keep execution tied to the original task, and review the resulting changes before they are merged.

The important distinction is that Sharkly coordinates the work while the coding agent performs it. Your existing model subscription or API account still handles model usage, and your team remains responsible for the quality and acceptance of the result.

I would start with one Jira project, one connected agent, and one low-risk ticket. Once the workflow is reliable, expand to more tasks and agents based on what your team actually needs.

That is a practical way to explore AI-assisted development without making a bigger investment in new AI tooling before you know whether the workflow delivers value.

articles.title: Claude Code Subagent Error Recovery in 2026: Retry Logic, Fallback Strategies, and Detecting Stuck Loops
articles.description: Error recovery determines whether your Claude Code subagents crash on transient failures or degrade gracefully. Learn retry logic, loop detection, and circuit breakers that prevent runaway costs.
articles.body_html:
Claude Code Subagent Error Recovery in 2026: Retry Logic, Fallback Strategies, and Detecting Stuck Loops

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most production agent failures trace back to a single omission: the absence of recovery logic. A subagent hits a rate limit, retries the same call immediately, burns through budget, and crashes the parent workflow. The coordinator receives a cryptic timeout after 90 seconds and has no idea which step failed or why.

Effective error recovery classifies failures by type, applies exponential backoff to transient issues, detects stuck loops before they drain budget, and propagates only the errors that require coordinator intervention. The difference shows up in uptime metrics and cost reports within days.

Key Takeaways

  • Transient failures (rate limits, network blips) require retry logic with exponential backoff; logical failures (invalid parameters) need immediate propagation.
  • Step repetition loops, where an agent retries identical tool calls, account for 15.7% of production failures and require hash-based detection.
  • Circuit breakers prevent runaway costs by halting agents that exceed token budgets or attempt thresholds before they exhaust resources.
  • Multi-agent systems should implement local recovery at the subagent level and propagate only errors the coordinator can resolve.
  • Fallback strategies like model switching or degraded responses keep workflows running when primary approaches fail.

Error Classification: Transient vs Logical vs Fatal

Error recovery begins with classification. Not all failures deserve the same response. A rate limit from the Anthropic API is transient and recoverable. A schema validation error in tool parameters is logical and permanent. A memory exhaustion crash is fatal and requires process restart.

Transient errors include network timeouts, temporary service unavailability, and quota limits. These failures resolve with time or retry attempts. Retry logic with exponential backoff handles them without human intervention.

Logical errors stem from incorrect inputs, malformed requests, or violated preconditions. The agent passed an invalid file path to a tool. The database query referenced a nonexistent column. Retrying the same call will produce the same failure. These errors require immediate propagation to the coordinator or user.

Fatal errors signal systemic problems: out-of-memory conditions, corrupted state, unrecoverable resource exhaustion. Recovery at the agent level is impossible. The process must terminate gracefully and report the failure upstream.

Teams that skip classification treat all errors identically. They retry logical failures until a timeout expires, wasting budget on calls guaranteed to fail. They give up on transient failures after a single attempt, reporting unavailability when a two-second wait would have succeeded.

The classification layer sits at the entry point of your error handler. Inspect the error type, status code, or message pattern. Route transient errors to retry logic, logical errors to validation logging, and fatal errors to graceful shutdown.

Building Retry Logic with Exponential Backoff

Exponential backoff prevents retry storms that amplify outages. When a rate limit hits, immediate retries pound the API harder and extend the unavailability window. Each retry doubles the wait time: 1 second, 2 seconds, 4 seconds, up to a maximum delay.

The implementation tracks attempt count, calculates delay with jitter, and enforces a maximum retry limit:

interface RetryConfig {
  maxAttempts: number;
  baseDelayMs: number;
  maxDelayMs: number;
  jitterFactor: number;
}

async function withRetry<T>(
  operation: () => Promise<T>,
  config: RetryConfig,
  isRetryable: (error: unknown) => boolean
): Promise<T> {
  let attempt = 0;

  while (attempt < config.maxAttempts) {
    try {
      return await operation();
    } catch (error) {
      attempt++;

      if (!isRetryable(error) || attempt >= config.maxAttempts) {
        throw error;
      }

      const exponentialDelay = config.baseDelayMs * Math.pow(2, attempt - 1);
      const jitter = exponentialDelay * config.jitterFactor * Math.random();
      const delayMs = Math.min(exponentialDelay + jitter, config.maxDelayMs);

      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    }
  }

  throw new Error("retry logic exhausted without success or terminal error");
}

function isTransientError(error: unknown): boolean {
  if (error instanceof Error) {
    const message = error.message.toLowerCase();
    return (
      message.includes("rate limit") ||
      message.includes("timeout") ||
      message.includes("503") ||
      message.includes("temporarily unavailable")
    );
  }
  return false;
}

const result = await withRetry(
  () => callClaudeAPI(prompt),
  { maxAttempts: 5, baseDelayMs: 1000, maxDelayMs: 16000, jitterFactor: 0.3 },
  isTransientError
);

Jitter randomizes delays across concurrent agents. Without jitter, all failed agents retry at identical intervals and create synchronized load spikes. Jitter spreads retries across a time window.

The isRetryable predicate prevents retry loops on logical errors. Check the error message, status code, or custom error class. Return false for validation failures, authentication errors, or missing resources.

Exponential backoff visualization showing delay curves with and without jitter

Teams that omit retry logic lose uptime to momentary glitches. A single network hiccup terminates the workflow. Teams that retry without backoff amplify failures and rack up costs during outages.

Detecting and Breaking Stuck Loops: The Step Repetition Problem

Step repetition loops occur when an agent retries identical tool calls without recognizing the pattern. The agent requests a file that does not exist, receives an error, and immediately requests the same file with the same path. After 20 iterations, the budget is exhausted and no progress has occurred.

Detection requires hashing each attempted step and tracking recent history. If the same hash appears three times in the last five steps, the agent is stuck:

interface StepAttempt {
  toolName: string;
  parameters: Record<string, unknown>;
  timestamp: number;
}

class LoopDetector {
  private history: string[] = [];
  private maxHistorySize = 10;
  private repetitionThreshold = 3;
  private lookbackWindow = 5;

  recordStep(step: StepAttempt): void {
    const hash = this.hashStep(step);
    this.history.push(hash);

    if (this.history.length > this.maxHistorySize) {
      this.history.shift();
    }
  }

  isStuck(): boolean {
    if (this.history.length < this.repetitionThreshold) {
      return false;
    }

    const recentSteps = this.history.slice(-this.lookbackWindow);
    const latestHash = recentSteps[recentSteps.length - 1];
    const matchCount = recentSteps.filter(h => h === latestHash).length;

    return matchCount >= this.repetitionThreshold;
  }

  private hashStep(step: StepAttempt): string {
    const normalized = JSON.stringify({
      tool: step.toolName,
      params: step.parameters
    });
    return this.simpleHash(normalized);
  }

  private simpleHash(str: string): string {
    let hash = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < str.length; i++) {
      const char = str.charCodeAt(i);
      hash = ((hash << 5) - hash) + char;
      hash = hash & hash;
    }
    return hash.toString(36);
  }

  reset(): void {
    this.history = [];
  }
}

const detector = new LoopDetector();

for (const step of agentSteps) {
  detector.recordStep(step);

  if (detector.isStuck()) {
    throw new Error(
      `agent stuck in repetition loop: attempted ${step.toolName} ` +
      `with identical parameters ${detector["repetitionThreshold"]} times`
    );
  }

  await executeStep(step);
}

The hash function normalizes tool name and parameters to catch semantic equivalence. Two calls with differently ordered JSON keys but identical content produce the same hash.

When a loop is detected, the agent must either request human intervention, switch to a fallback approach, or terminate the workflow with a descriptive error. Continuing execution wastes resources and delays failure diagnosis.

Some loops arise from environment state. The agent checks if a file exists, finds it missing, attempts to create it, and the creation fails silently. The next iteration repeats the check and creation. Loop detection surfaces the underlying issue: file creation permissions are missing.

Teams that ignore loop detection discover stuck agents hours later when budget alerts fire. The agent consumed $200 in tokens retrying a single failed operation. The workflow never progressed past step two.

Fallback Strategies: Model Switching and Degraded Responses

When primary recovery fails, fallback strategies keep workflows running at reduced capacity. Model switching drops to a cheaper or faster model when the primary model is unavailable. Degraded responses return partial results instead of failing completely.

Model switching maintains a priority list. If Claude 3.5 Sonnet hits rate limits, the coordinator switches to Claude 3 Haiku for less critical subagents. The workflow continues with reduced accuracy but meets the deadline:

interface ModelConfig {
  modelId: string;
  priority: number;
  costPerToken: number;
  maxTokens: number;
}

class ModelFallbackStrategy {
  private models: ModelConfig[] = [
    { modelId: "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022", priority: 1, costPerToken: 0.003, maxTokens: 200000 },
    { modelId: "claude-3-5-haiku-20241022", priority: 2, costPerToken: 0.0008, maxTokens: 200000 },
    { modelId: "claude-3-haiku-20240307", priority: 3, costPerToken: 0.00025, maxTokens: 200000 }
  ];

  private currentIndex = 0;

  async callWithFallback<T>(
    operation: (modelId: string) => Promise<T>
  ): Promise<T> {
    while (this.currentIndex < this.models.length) {
      const model = this.models[this.currentIndex];

      try {
        return await operation(model.modelId);
      } catch (error) {
        if (this.shouldFallback(error) && this.currentIndex < this.models.length - 1) {
          console.warn(
            `model ${model.modelId} failed, falling back to ${this.models[this.currentIndex + 1].modelId}`
          );
          this.currentIndex++;
        } else {
          throw error;
        }
      }
    }

    throw new Error("all fallback models exhausted");
  }

  private shouldFallback(error: unknown): boolean {
    if (error instanceof Error) {
      const message = error.message.toLowerCase();
      return (
        message.includes("rate limit") ||
        message.includes("overloaded") ||
        message.includes("503")
      );
    }
    return false;
  }

  reset(): void {
    this.currentIndex = 0;
  }
}

const strategy = new ModelFallbackStrategy();

const response = await strategy.callWithFallback(async (modelId) => {
  return await anthropic.messages.create({
    model: modelId,
    max_tokens: 4096,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: prompt }]
  });
});

Degraded responses return partial data when complete results are unavailable. A document summarization agent that cannot access three of ten source files returns a summary of the seven it processed, along with a warning about missing sources.

The key decision: when does partial success outweigh complete failure? If the workflow is time-critical and 70% accuracy suffices, degraded responses are appropriate. If correctness is paramount, fail fast and propagate the error.

Model fallback cascade showing priority tiers from Sonnet to Haiku

Teams that lack fallback strategies experience all-or-nothing availability. A single rate limit brings down the entire multi-agent system. Teams with fallback strategies maintain partial functionality during degraded conditions and meet deadlines that rigid systems miss.

Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems

Subagents should recover locally from transient failures before propagating errors to the coordinator. Only errors that require coordinator intervention or represent unrecoverable logical failures should propagate upward.

A file processing subagent that encounters a rate-limited API call retries with exponential backoff. If retries succeed, the coordinator never learns about the transient failure. If all retries fail, the subagent propagates a structured error with context:

Error objects must carry sufficient context for the coordinator to make informed decisions. Include the subagent ID, the failed operation, relevant parameters, and prior recovery attempts:

interface SubagentError {
  subagentId: string;
  operation: string;
  parameters: Record<string, unknown>;
  originalError: string;
  retryAttempts: number;
  recoveryStrategy: string;
  timestamp: number;
}

class Subagent {
  private id: string;
  private retryConfig: RetryConfig;

  async executeTask(task: Task): Promise<TaskResult> {
    try {
      return await withRetry(
        () => this.performTask(task),
        this.retryConfig,
        isTransientError
      );
    } catch (error) {
      const structured: SubagentError = {
        subagentId: this.id,
        operation: task.operation,
        parameters: task.parameters,
        originalError: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error),
        retryAttempts: this.retryConfig.maxAttempts,
        recoveryStrategy: "exponential backoff",
        timestamp: Date.now()
      };

      throw structured;
    }
  }

  private async performTask(task: Task): Promise<TaskResult> {
    // actual task execution
    return { status: "completed", data: {} };
  }
}

class Coordinator {
  async orchestrate(subagents: Subagent[], tasks: Task[]): Promise<void> {
    const results = await Promise.allSettled(
      tasks.map((task, i) => subagents[i].executeTask(task))
    );

    for (const result of results) {
      if (result.status === "rejected") {
        const error = result.reason as SubagentError;

        if (this.canCompensate(error)) {
          await this.applyCompensation(error);
        } else {
          throw new Error(
            `unrecoverable subagent failure: ${error.subagentId} ` +
            `failed ${error.operation} after ${error.retryAttempts} attempts`
          );
        }
      }
    }
  }

  private canCompensate(error: SubagentError): boolean {
    return error.operation === "fetch_optional_data";
  }

  private async applyCompensation(error: SubagentError): Promise<void> {
    console.log(`compensating for optional operation failure: ${error.operation}`);
  }
}

The coordinator inspects each error and decides whether to retry with a different subagent, apply a compensation strategy, or fail the entire workflow. Optional operations that fail may warrant compensation rather than termination.

Correlation IDs link errors across agent boundaries. When a subagent propagates an error, it includes the correlation ID from the originating request. The coordinator can trace the failure back through the call chain and identify the root cause. For more on correlation IDs in agent systems, see correlation IDs for AI agents.

Teams that propagate every error overwhelm coordinators with noise. Transient failures that resolve locally should remain invisible. Teams that swallow all errors at the subagent level leave coordinators blind to systemic issues.

Circuit Breakers and Budget Caps for Runaway Agents

Circuit breakers prevent runaway agents from exhausting budgets or API quotas. When an agent exceeds a token threshold or failure count, the circuit breaker trips and halts execution before damage compounds.

Token budget tracking measures cumulative token usage. When usage exceeds 80% of the allocated budget, the circuit breaker issues a warning. At 100%, it terminates the agent:

interface CircuitBreakerConfig {
  tokenBudget: number;
  maxFailures: number;
  resetTimeoutMs: number;
}

enum CircuitState {
  CLOSED = "closed",
  OPEN = "open",
  HALF_OPEN = "half_open"
}

class CircuitBreaker {
  private state = CircuitState.CLOSED;
  private tokenUsage = 0;
  private failures = 0;
  private lastFailureTime = 0;

  constructor(private config: CircuitBreakerConfig) {}

  recordTokens(count: number): void {
    this.tokenUsage += count;

    const usagePercent = (this.tokenUsage / this.config.tokenBudget) * 100;

    if (usagePercent >= 80 && usagePercent < 100) {
      console.warn(`circuit breaker warning: ${usagePercent.toFixed(1)}% of token budget consumed`);
    }

    if (this.tokenUsage >= this.config.tokenBudget) {
      this.trip("token budget exceeded");
    }
  }

  recordFailure(): void {
    this.failures++;
    this.lastFailureTime = Date.now();

    if (this.failures >= this.config.maxFailures) {
      this.trip("max failures exceeded");
    }
  }

  recordSuccess(): void {
    if (this.state === CircuitState.HALF_OPEN) {
      this.reset();
    }
  }

  async execute<T>(operation: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    if (this.state === CircuitState.OPEN) {
      if (Date.now() - this.lastFailureTime >= this.config.resetTimeoutMs) {
        this.state = CircuitState.HALF_OPEN;
      } else {
        throw new Error("circuit breaker is open, rejecting operation");
      }
    }

    try {
      const result = await operation();
      this.recordSuccess();
      return result;
    } catch (error) {
      this.recordFailure();
      throw error;
    }
  }

  private trip(reason: string): void {
    this.state = CircuitState.OPEN;
    console.error(`circuit breaker tripped: ${reason}`);
    throw new Error(`circuit breaker open: ${reason}`);
  }

  private reset(): void {
    this.state = CircuitState.CLOSED;
    this.failures = 0;
    console.info("circuit breaker reset to closed state");
  }

  getStatus() {
    return {
      state: this.state,
      tokenUsage: this.tokenUsage,
      tokenBudget: this.config.tokenBudget,
      failures: this.failures,
      maxFailures: this.config.maxFailures
    };
  }
}

const breaker = new CircuitBreaker({
  tokenBudget: 50000,
  maxFailures: 5,
  resetTimeoutMs: 60000
});

for (const task of tasks) {
  await breaker.execute(async () => {
    const response = await callClaudeAPI(task.prompt);
    breaker.recordTokens(response.usage.input_tokens + response.usage.output_tokens);
    return response;
  });
}

The half-open state tests recovery. After the reset timeout expires, the circuit breaker allows a single operation. If it succeeds, the circuit fully resets. If it fails, the circuit trips again and waits for another timeout.

Rate limit guards complement circuit breakers by enforcing request-per-minute caps. If an agent attempts more than 60 API calls per minute, the guard delays subsequent calls:

class RateLimitGuard {
  private requests: number[] = [];
  private windowMs = 60000;
  private maxRequests = 60;

  async acquire(): Promise<void> {
    const now = Date.now();
    this.requests = this.requests.filter(t => now - t < this.windowMs);

    if (this.requests.length >= this.maxRequests) {
      const oldestRequest = this.requests[0];
      const delayMs = this.windowMs - (now - oldestRequest);
      await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      return this.acquire();
    }

    this.requests.push(now);
  }
}

Teams that skip circuit breakers discover runaway agents when the monthly bill arrives. A single stuck agent consumed $2,000 in tokens because no guard halted execution. Teams with circuit breakers catch runaway conditions within seconds and cap losses at predefined thresholds.

For more on managing agent environments and secrets that influence error scenarios, see environment and secrets management for Claude Code subagents.

Frequently Asked Questions

What retry delay should I use for rate-limited API calls?

Start with a base delay of 1 second and double it for each attempt up to a maximum of 16 seconds. Add 30% jitter to prevent synchronized retries across concurrent agents. Most transient rate limits resolve within 5 to 10 seconds.

How do I prevent agents from retrying logical errors that will never succeed?

Classify errors by inspecting status codes, error messages, or custom error types. Return false from the isRetryable predicate for validation failures, authentication errors, and resource-not-found conditions. Only retry transient failures like timeouts, 503 responses, and temporary unavailability.

When should a subagent propagate an error to the coordinator instead of recovering locally?

Propagate errors that the subagent cannot resolve through retry logic or fallback strategies: authentication failures, missing required resources, exceeded token budgets, or logical errors in the task specification. Recover locally from transient network issues, rate limits, and temporary service unavailability.

How do I detect step repetition loops in agents that use different parameter values each attempt?

Hash the combination of tool name and normalized parameters. Two calls with identical tool and parameters produce the same hash even if parameter order differs. If the same hash appears three or more times in the last five steps, the agent is stuck in a repetition loop.

What token budget should I allocate per subagent to prevent runaway costs?

Allocate budgets based on task complexity and expected length. Simple classification tasks may need 5,000 tokens. Document generation tasks may require 50,000 tokens. Set the budget at 150% of typical usage and configure circuit breakers to trip at 100% to prevent overruns.

Conclusion

Error recovery separates production-ready agents from prototypes. Retry logic with exponential backoff recovers from transient failures without amplifying load. Loop detection catches stuck agents before they exhaust budgets. Circuit breakers halt runaway processes before costs spiral. Structured error propagation gives coordinators the context they need to compensate or fail gracefully.

The agents that survive production are the ones that expect failure, classify it accurately, and recover without human intervention. For more on packaging reusable recovery logic, see packaging and distribution guide for Claude Code plugins. Start with classification, add retry logic to transient paths, and install circuit breakers before the first deployment. The failures you handle gracefully never reach your incident log.

articles.title: You should use Map instead of object literals for lookup tables
articles.description: A while ago I wrote an article about using object literals instead of switch statements, and I still...
articles.body_html:
A while ago I wrote an article about using object literals instead of switch statements, and I still think the idea behind it is a good one: map an input to an output, skip the long list of case and break, and keep your code short and readable.

But there's a catch I didn't cover back then, and a reader (thanks Dario!) pointed it out in the comments: plain objects don't only contain the keys you put in them.

So in this article I want to show you what the problem is, and why today I'd reach for a Map instead.

A quick recap

In the previous article we had something like this:

const getAnimalSound = animal => {
  const sounds = {
    dog: 'woof',
    cat: 'meow',
    cow: 'moo',
    default: 'unknown sound',
  };

  return sounds[animal] || sounds.default;
};

console.log(getAnimalSound('dog'));   // 'woof'
console.log(getAnimalSound('tiger')); // 'unknown sound'

Clean, short, and it works. Or at least it looks like it does.

So what's the problem?

Every object you create with {} inherits from Object.prototype. This means that when you read sounds[animal], if JavaScript doesn't find the key on the object itself, it goes up the prototype chain and looks there too.

And Object.prototype has quite a few properties on it, like constructor, toString, valueOf, hasOwnProperty and __proto__.

Let's see what happens if we pass one of those names to our function:

console.log(getAnimalSound('constructor')); // [Function: Object]
console.log(getAnimalSound('toString'));    // [Function: toString]
console.log(getAnimalSound('__proto__'));   // [Object: null prototype] {}

None of those return 'unknown sound'. Because the value we get back is truthy, the || sounds.default fallback never kicks in, and we return something completely unexpected.

Now, you might think "who would ever pass constructor as an animal?". And you are probably right, until that value comes from a query string, a form field, or the body of an API request. Then anybody can pass whatever they want.

It gets worse with functions

In the previous article we also used object literals to dispatch commands:

const executeCommand = command => {
  const commands = {
    greet: () => console.log('Hello there!'),
    farewell: () => console.log('Goodbye!'),
    default: () => console.log('Unknown command'),
  };

  (commands[command] || commands.default)();
};

Let's try a few "commands":

executeCommand('constructor');    // nothing happens, it silently calls Object()
executeCommand('toString');       // nothing happens either
executeCommand('hasOwnProperty'); // TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object

The first two fail silently, which is the worst kind of bug, because you don't even know something went wrong. The last one crashes your function.

And with nested objects

The state machine example is my favourite one:

const stateTransitions = {
  idle: { start: 'loading' },
  loading: { success: 'loaded', error: 'error' },
};

const handleStateTransition = (currentState, action) =>
  stateTransitions[currentState]?.[action] || currentState;

console.log(handleStateTransition('constructor', 'name')); // 'Object'
console.log(handleStateTransition('idle', 'toString'));    // [Function: toString]

Yes, your component is now in the 'Object' state, or worse, its state is a function.

Note
To be clear, this is not prototype pollution. Prototype pollution happens when an attacker manages to write to Object.prototype, for example with obj[key] = value where key is __proto__. Here we are only reading, but it's still a real bug, and it's the reason why security linters like eslint-plugin-security flag obj[variable] lookups.

Enter Map

A Map is a built-in collection of key/value pairs, and the important difference is that map.get(key) only returns entries that you explicitly added. There's no prototype chain to walk through, so constructor is just a key like any other, and since you never added it, you get undefined.

Let's rewrite our first example:

const sounds = new Map([
  ['dog', 'woof'],
  ['cat', 'meow'],
  ['cow', 'moo'],
]);

const getAnimalSound = animal => sounds.get(animal) ?? 'unknown sound';

console.log(getAnimalSound('dog'));         // 'woof'
console.log(getAnimalSound('tiger'));       // 'unknown sound'
console.log(getAnimalSound('constructor')); // 'unknown sound' ✅
console.log(getAnimalSound('__proto__'));   // 'unknown sound' ✅

You might have noticed a few other small changes, and they are not random:

  • The Map is defined outside the function, so we don't rebuild it every time the function is called.
  • The fallback is no longer stored as a default key, so nobody can "select" it by passing 'default'.
  • I'm using ?? (nullish coalescing) instead of ||. With ||, a valid value like 0 or an empty string would be replaced by the fallback. With ??, the fallback is used only when the value is null or undefined.

Tip
If you already have an object and you don't want to rewrite it as an array of arrays, you can convert it with new Map(Object.entries(myObject)).

Dispatching functions

The same works for our commands:

const commands = new Map([
  ['greet', () => console.log('Hello there!')],
  ['farewell', () => console.log('Goodbye!')],
  ['time', () => console.log(`Current time: ${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}`)],
]);

const unknownCommand = () => console.log('Unknown command');

const executeCommand = command => (commands.get(command) ?? unknownCommand)();

executeCommand('greet');          // 'Hello there!'
executeCommand('hasOwnProperty'); // 'Unknown command' ✅

And with parameters, like the calculator from the previous article:

const operations = new Map([
  ['add', (x, y) => x + y],
  ['subtract', (x, y) => x - y],
  ['multiply', (x, y) => x * y],
  ['divide', (x, y) => (y !== 0 ? x / y : 'Cannot divide by zero')],
]);

const calculator = (a, b, operation) => {
  const fn = operations.get(operation);
  return fn ? fn(a, b) : 'Unknown operation';
};

console.log(calculator(5, 3, 'add'));     // 8
console.log(calculator(5, 3, 'valueOf')); // 'Unknown operation' ✅

The state machine

For nested lookups you can nest Maps too:

const stateTransitions = new Map([
  ['idle', new Map([['start', 'loading'], ['reset', 'idle']])],
  ['loading', new Map([['success', 'loaded'], ['error', 'error'], ['cancel', 'idle']])],
  ['loaded', new Map([['refresh', 'loading'], ['clear', 'idle']])],
  ['error', new Map([['retry', 'loading'], ['clear', 'idle']])],
]);

const handleStateTransition = (currentState, action) =>
  stateTransitions.get(currentState)?.get(action) ?? currentState;

let state = 'idle';
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'start');    // 'loading'
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'success');  // 'loaded'
state = handleStateTransition(state, 'toString'); // 'loaded' (unchanged) ✅

I'll be honest, this one is a bit less pretty than the object version. We'll come back to that in a moment.

A bonus with TypeScript

If you use TypeScript, Map has another nice side effect: map.get() always returns T | undefined, so the compiler forces you to handle the missing case.

type Animal = 'dog' | 'cat' | 'cow';

const sounds = new Map<Animal, string>([
  ['dog', 'woof'],
  ['cat', 'meow'],
  ['cow', 'moo'],
]);

const getAnimalSound = (animal: Animal): string =>
  sounds.get(animal) ?? 'unknown sound'; // without ?? TypeScript will complain

When you don't need a Map

As always, I don't want you to take this as "never use objects again". There are cases where a plain object is perfectly fine.

When the keys never come from outside your code. If the key is a value you control, for example a TypeScript literal union that you pass around internally, the prototype issue can't really happen. In that case an object with satisfies gives you great type checking:

type Animal = 'dog' | 'cat' | 'cow';

const sounds = {
  dog: 'woof',
  cat: 'meow',
  cow: 'moo',
} satisfies Record<Animal, string>;

Just remember that TypeScript types disappear at runtime: if the value comes from a request or a form, you still need to validate it.

When you only need a quick safety check. If you want to keep the object syntax, Object.hasOwn() checks only the object's own properties, ignoring the prototype chain:

const getAnimalSound = animal =>
  Object.hasOwn(sounds, animal) ? sounds[animal] : 'unknown sound';

This is also a good option for deeply nested tables like the state machine, where nested Maps get a bit noisy.

When you need to serialise the data. JSON.stringify(new Map([['a', 1]])) returns {}, not what you expect. If your lookup table needs to be sent over the wire or saved as JSON, an object is easier to work with.

When switch is simply the better tool. As I mentioned in the previous article, if your conditions involve ranges, complex expressions or intentional fall-through, a switch is still the right choice.

Conclusions

Object literals are still a great idea to replace long switch statements, but when the key comes from user input, a plain object can return things you never put in it, like constructor or toString.

A Map fixes that by design: it only knows the keys you gave it, it works nicely with ??, and with TypeScript it forces you to handle the missing case.

So my rule of thumb today is simple:

  • If the key comes from outside your code, use a Map.
  • If the key is fully under your control, an object is fine, and Object.hasOwn() is a cheap safety net if you want one.

I hope this helped you to understand the hidden gotcha of object lookups, and as always any comments are welcome!

Parts of this article were created with the help of AI.
