Why Your React Animations Feel Slow Even at 60 FPS

You open the Performance panel. The animation is running around 60 FPS. There are no spectacular red warnings, nothing is visibly freezing, and your laptop is barely interested.

Yet the interaction still feels slow.

The cursor seems to chase the pointer instead of following it. A scroll reveal arrives just after you expect it. A draggable card has a slightly rubbery disconnect from your hand. A menu technically animates smoothly, but opening it feels heavier than clicking the same control without motion.

This is where an FPS counter can send debugging in the wrong direction.

60 FPS tells you how many frames arrived. It does not tell you whether they arrived well.

Animation quality is a combination of frame consistency, input latency, browser rendering work, JavaScript execution and the actual motion decisions you made. React can participate in those problems, but “React is slow” is rarely a useful diagnosis.

The better question is: what kind of slow are you looking at?

60 FPS Is a Target, Not a Diagnosis

On a 60 Hz display, the browser gets a new refresh opportunity roughly every 16.7 milliseconds. During that window it may need to execute JavaScript, recalculate styles, perform layout, paint pixels and composite layers before the updated frame reaches the display.

That is why 60 FPS became a familiar target for interface animation. A consistently delivered frame roughly every 16.7 ms can look smooth on a 60 Hz display.

The important word is consistently.

Imagine an FPS overlay reports an average around 60 over a measurement window. That number does not tell you whether individual frames were evenly spaced. A sequence with occasional slow frames followed by quicker frames can have a respectable average while still producing visible hitching.

Perceived motion follows the spacing of frames, not the optimism of the average.

This is also why hardcoding your animation around an assumption of exactly 60 updates per second is fragile. Displays running at 120 Hz and 144 Hz are common enough that requestAnimationFrame() may be called at those rates instead. MDN explicitly recommends using the timestamp provided to the callback when calculating animation progress.

let start;

function animate(timestamp) {
  if (start === undefined) {
    start = timestamp;
  }

  const elapsed = timestamp - start;
  const progress = Math.min(elapsed / 600, 1);

  element.style.transform = `translateX(${progress * 200}px)`;

  if (progress < 1) {
    requestAnimationFrame(animate);
  }
}

requestAnimationFrame(animate);

The animation above is based on elapsed time rather than “move three pixels every frame.” That distinction keeps the duration stable when the display refresh rate changes.

You can read more about the behavior of requestAnimationFrame() on MDN.

Your Browser Has More Work to Do Than Draw the Animation

When an element changes visually, the browser does not simply receive your new value and teleport pixels into place.

Depending on what changed, it can move through several stages: style recalculation, layout, paint and composition. The amount of work depends partly on the CSS property being animated.

Animating something that changes geometry, such as width, left or margin, can require the browser to recalculate layout and repaint. Properties such as transform and opacity can often avoid layout and be handled later in the rendering pipeline.

Consider a simple horizontal movement.

// Can require layout work as the value changes
<div style={{ left: `${x}px` }} />

// Usually a better fit for visual movement
<div style={{ transform: `translateX(${x}px)` }} />

That does not mean transform is a magic performance keyword. You can animate only transforms and still build a sluggish interaction if each frame also performs expensive JavaScript, reads layout repeatedly, updates a large React subtree, draws an expensive canvas scene or runs several competing effects.

The property is one part of the frame. MDN has a useful breakdown of the browser rendering waterfall and animation property costs.

The practical debugging question is not just “Am I getting 60 FPS?” It is “What work has to complete before each visible update?”

React Can Make the Animation Compete With Your Application

React state is a great way to express application state. It is not automatically the best place to store every intermediate pixel of an animation. Suppose a pointer-following element writes its coordinates into component state for every pointermove event:

import { useState } from "react";

export default function Follower() {
  const [position, setPosition] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });

  return (
    <div
      onPointerMove={(event) => {
        setPosition({
          x: event.clientX,
          y: event.clientY,
        });
      }}
    >
      <div
        className="follower"
        style={{
          transform: `translate3d(${position.x}px, ${position.y}px, 0)`,
        }}
      />
    </div>
  );
}

There is nothing inherently invalid about this code. The relevant question is what happens around it.

Every state update schedules React work. If Follower is isolated and the surrounding tree is cheap, the result may be perfectly acceptable. If the update causes substantial component work while other JavaScript is also running, you have made your animation share main-thread time with work that may not need to happen every frame.

For transient per-frame values, a ref or an animation system can sometimes keep React responsible for the meaningful state transition while letting interpolation happen outside repeated component renders.

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

export default function Follower() {
  const followerRef = useRef(null);
  const target = useRef({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  const current = useRef({ x: 0, y: 0 });

  useEffect(() => {
    let frameId;

    const tick = () => {
      current.current.x +=
        (target.current.x - current.current.x) * 0.18;

      current.current.y +=
        (target.current.y - current.current.y) * 0.18;

      if (followerRef.current) {
        followerRef.current.style.transform =
          `translate3d(${current.current.x}px, ${current.current.y}px, 0)`;
      }

      frameId = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    };

    frameId = requestAnimationFrame(tick);

    return () => cancelAnimationFrame(frameId);
  }, []);

  return (
    <div
      onPointerMove={(event) => {
        target.current.x = event.clientX;
        target.current.y = event.clientY;
      }}
    >
      <div ref={followerRef} className="follower" />
    </div>
  );
}

This is not a rule that says “never animate through React state.” It is a separation-of-responsibilities question.

If a value exists mainly to produce another visual frame a few milliseconds later, ask whether the entire React render path needs to know about every intermediate value.

Profile before rewriting it.

requestAnimationFrame() Does Not Make Expensive Work Cheap

Moving code into requestAnimationFrame() is another optimization that can feel more powerful than it is.

requestAnimationFrame() tells the browser you want to run a callback before an upcoming repaint. It gives your animation work a browser-aware scheduling mechanism. It does not reduce the amount of work inside the callback.

This can still be expensive:

function tick() {
  const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".card");

  cards.forEach((card) => {
    const rect = card.getBoundingClientRect();

    card.style.transform =
      `translateY(${window.innerHeight - rect.top}px)`;
  });

  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}

requestAnimationFrame(tick);

Now you are querying elements, measuring layout and writing styles repeatedly. Put enough work in there and rAF will faithfully schedule an expensive callback every time the browser gives you the chance.

The useful question is:

What am I asking the browser to do inside each frame?

Cache what can be cached. Avoid unnecessary layout measurement inside hot loops. Keep cleanup explicit. Stop loops that no longer have a reason to run.

requestAnimationFrame() is a scheduler, not absolution.

Sometimes the Performance Problem Is Actually a Motion Problem

This is the category that profiling tools cannot solve for you. An interaction can be computationally cheap, maintain a steady frame rate and still feel slow because you told it to move slowly.

Imagine a cursor follower using this interpolation:

current += (target - current) * 0.05;

The browser may render it beautifully. No dropped frames. No expensive layout. No large React commits. It can still feel like the cursor is dragging a reluctant ghost behind it.

Change the interpolation:

current += (target - current) * 0.22;

The computational cost is effectively the same, but the interaction feels radically more immediate.

The same problem appears with animation durations, easing curves and springs. A navigation overlay with a long ease-in can feel resistant because the first part of the motion barely moves. A spring with too little stiffness or too much settling can make a button feel mushy. A parallax layer that deliberately trails scroll position may cross the line from depth into input lag.

A perfectly rendered delay is still a delay.

This matters because developers often respond to that feeling by optimizing code that is already fast enough. They memoize components, switch libraries or reach for will-change, only to discover that the animation still feels heavy.

Before doing that, temporarily shorten the duration or remove smoothing. If the interaction suddenly feels right while the performance trace barely changes, you found a motion-design problem rather than a rendering bottleneck.

Input-Coupled Motion Exposes Latency Faster

Not all animation has the same relationship with the user.

A decorative background can arrive slightly late without anyone having a precise expectation for where it should be. A button pressed under a cursor is different. So is dragging, scrolling, scrubbing or moving a custom pointer.

The user's hand provides a reference signal.

If their pointer is here and your visual follower is consistently there, the delay is obvious. If their finger moves a card and the card takes time to catch up, they feel the gap before they think about it technically.

This is why scroll smoothing deserves restraint. Smoothing the visual response can create a deliberate sense of weight, but too much of it makes the page feel as though scrolling has been routed through syrup.

The same applies to cursor trails. A trailing layer can be expressive while the actual clickable interaction remains immediate. Trouble starts when decorative latency leaks into controls that are supposed to feel direct. For input-driven effects, profile responsiveness and inspect your interpolation before chasing raw FPS.

“Use Transform and Opacity” Is Good Advice With Missing Footnotes

For many DOM animations, transform and opacity are sensible first choices because they can avoid the layout work triggered by geometry-changing properties. They should not become a superstition.

A fullscreen blur, huge translucent layer, complex SVG filter, large shadow or high-resolution canvas may still cost real rendering time even if its position changes through transform. A page running five independently smooth animation loops can become expensive when they all operate together.

Production pages are ecosystems. Your effect does not get a private browser.

This becomes especially noticeable on marketing sites where animation lives beside analytics, hydration, images, video, sliders, third-party scripts and application code. An isolated CodePen can tell you whether the effect works. It cannot tell you what happens after the effect moves into the page that has to ship.

Profile Frame Time, Not Just the Counter

When an animation feels wrong, resist the urge to start changing code randomly.

Reproduce the issue in the environment where it actually matters. Use a production build when possible. Development tooling and extra checks can distort performance characteristics.

Then record the interaction in your browser's Performance panel.

Look at what is occupying the main thread around the problematic frames. Is there a large JavaScript task? Repeated style recalculation? Layout work? Expensive paint? A React render arriving at exactly the wrong moment? Multiple callbacks continuing after their sections have left the viewport?

You are trying to identify a category of failure before choosing a fix.

A useful diagnostic table looks like this:

What you feel Inspect first
Animation visibly jumps Frame timing, long JavaScript tasks, layout and paint
Motion is smooth but follows input late Smoothing, interpolation, input handling and main-thread work
Animation struggles while UI data changes React renders and competing JavaScript
Works on desktop, struggles on phone CPU/GPU cost, image/canvas work and concurrent effects
Smooth everywhere but still feels heavy Duration, easing, distance and spring tuning

For deeper diagnostics, browsers are also gaining visibility into Long Animation Frames, which can help identify work contributing to long frames. Treat it as an additional signal rather than the one universal profiling API; support and tooling still deserve checking for your target browsers.

Test the Page, Not the Demo

An animation should be judged in the page where it will live.

That means testing it beside the real navigation, typography, images, scripts and adjacent interactions. It also means testing the actual devices you care about rather than using a high-end development machine as your minimum specification.

Mobile changes more than available processing power. Pointer assumptions disappear. Viewports become shorter. Touch scrolling behaves differently. Effects that feel appropriately restrained with a mouse can become annoying when attached to every finger movement.

Offscreen work matters too. If a canvas render loop or animation keeps producing frames after the user has left the section, it is still spending resources even though it contributes nothing to the current experience.

The production checklist is therefore broader than “does it hit 60?”

Ask whether the effect stops when appropriate. Ask whether it still reads correctly without motion. Check prefers-reduced-motion where the interaction calls for an alternative. Verify keyboard and touch behavior where controls are involved.

And test the whole page.

Source Access Is Useful Because Performance Decisions Are Contextual

This is also where reusable animation patterns get interesting.

A polished demo can give you the right interaction idea, but production usually requires changing something: timing, breakpoint behavior, scroll distance, pointer behavior, dependencies, cleanup, the number of animated elements, or what happens when motion is reduced.

That is why Hyperiux Vault uses a source-first model for its React and Next.js interaction effects. The effect files land in your project, so the implementation can be inspected and tuned rather than treated as a sealed animation runtime. That does not make an effect automatically fast. It makes the decisions visible.

A scroll interaction may need different behavior on a short mobile viewport. A cursor system should not assume a fine pointer exists on every device. A WebGL scene has a very different rendering budget from a CSS text reveal. Those decisions belong in the implementation, not in a blanket promise that every animation is “optimized.”

Vault's Scroll Effects guidance makes the same production distinction: use properties appropriate for animation, avoid unnecessary layout reads during scroll, clean up timelines and listeners, and test the effect on a real mid-range device before treating the implementation as finished.

If you want a starting point rather than another empty component file, you can browse the React and Next.js interaction effects in Vault and adapt the source to the page that actually has to ship.

A Better Way to Debug “Slow” Animation

The next time an animation looks smooth in an FPS overlay but feels wrong under your hand, split the problem into separate questions.

Is the browser delivering frames consistently? Is expensive work happening during those frames? Is React doing work that does not need to happen at animation frequency? Is the visual response arriving late after input? Or is the easing itself simply telling the interface to feel slow?

Those failures can look similar from the outside, but they need different fixes.

60 FPS is useful evidence. It just isn't a verdict.

articles.title: Your Custom Hooks Tear in React 18. `useSyncExternalStore` Fixes It.
articles.description: A useState + useEffect hook that subscribes to window size, localStorage, or a WebSocket looks fine until React 18's concurrent rendering shows two parts of your UI two different values at once. useSyncExternalStore is the hook built to stop that.
articles.body_html:
The header says "You're offline." Three pixels below it, the save button is still clickable, sending requests like nothing's wrong. Same navigator.onLine value. Same render. Two different answers on screen at the same time.

You didn't write a new bug. You wrote the hook everyone writes.

function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine);

  useEffect(() => {
    const update = () => setOnline(navigator.onLine);
    window.addEventListener('online', update);
    window.addEventListener('offline', update);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('online', update);
      window.removeEventListener('offline', update);
    };
  }, []);

  return online;
}

It worked in every app you shipped before React 18. Then a teammate wraps a route transition in startTransition to keep the UI responsive, two components that both call useOnlineStatus() briefly disagree, and you spend an afternoon adding console.log statements to a bug that reproduces maybe one time in fifteen.

Why a perfectly normal hook starts lying

useState + useEffect assumes something React 18 no longer guarantees: that once a component commits, it stays committed until the next explicit update, and that every component re-renders from the same world.

Concurrent rendering breaks that assumption on purpose. React can start rendering a tree, pause partway through to handle something more urgent — a keystroke, a transition — and resume later. If the external value your hook reads (navigator.onLine, window.innerWidth, a value in localStorage, a WebSocket payload) changes in that gap, some components finish rendering with the old value and some with the new one. Nothing crashes. You just get a UI where two places disagree about one fact, for one frame, with no error to catch.

This has a name: tearing. It's not a React bug — it's the cost of letting renders be interruptible, and it only shows up once a render can be interrupted.

The hook was never wrong before — it was just never tested like this

Here's the part that catches people: useState + useEffect isn't a bad pattern. It's the correct pattern for state React owns. The problem is specifically external state — state that lives outside React and changes on its own schedule, which is exactly what "subscribe to a browser API" always is.

A useEffect-based subscription updates state after the store already changed, through a callback, on React's own timing. It has no way to ask, right before this component paints, "is this still current?" It just trusts whatever setOnline it last received.

The fix React shipped for exactly this

useSyncExternalStore is the hook React 18 added so you stop hand-rolling this. The shape is unusual the first time you see it — three functions, no state:

import { useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';

function subscribe(callback) {
  window.addEventListener('online', callback);
  window.addEventListener('offline', callback);
  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener('online', callback);
    window.removeEventListener('offline', callback);
  };
}

function getSnapshot() {
  return navigator.onLine;
}

function useOnlineStatus() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot);
}

subscribe wires up your listener once, same as the useEffect before. The difference is getSnapshot — a function that reads the current value directly, with nothing cached in React state. React calls it on every render, and critically, it re-checks it synchronously right before committing. If the store moved since the last check, React throws that render away and re-renders immediately with the fresh value, instead of letting a stale one paint. That synchronous re-check is the whole fix: it closes the exact gap where tearing happens.

You're not writing less code than before. You're handing React the one piece of information — "read it fresh, right now" — that a useState callback can never provide after the fact.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that bites on the server

useSyncExternalStore takes an optional third argument, getServerSnapshot, and skipping it is the next trap:

function getServerSnapshot() {
  return true; // sensible default: assume online during SSR
}

useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot);

There's no window on the server, so getSnapshot can't run there — navigator doesn't exist. If your component can render during SSR and you omit getServerSnapshot, React throws rather than guessing. It's not being pedantic: without it, the server-rendered HTML and the first client render would read different realities, and React would rather fail loudly than ship a hydration mismatch silently.

If your component is client-only (inside a dynamic import with SSR disabled, say), you can skip it. If it ever renders on the server, you can't.

You've already used this, you just didn't call it

If you reach for Zustand or react-redux (v8+), you're already running on useSyncExternalStore — it's what those libraries' React bindings switched to for exactly this reason. (Jotai, notably, chose not to — its author has written publicly about trading a small tearing risk for behavior that fits Suspense better.) You don't need to rewrite a working store library. You need this hook for the stores you wrote yourself: the useLocalStorage, useMediaQuery, or useWebSocketMessage hook sitting in your hooks/ folder, quietly subscribing to something outside React with a pattern that was correct until concurrent rendering gave it a seam to fall through.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 6-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Go find your oldest useState + useEffect-plus-addEventListener hook. If it feeds more than one component, it has a tearing window — you just haven't hit the one render that exposes it yet. What's yours tracking: window size, online status, something else? Tell me in the comments and I'll tell you if it needs the swap.

articles.title: In an AI security audit, the skeptic is the product
articles.description: I wrote four security findings against a 47-line Node service. Two of them were false. One cites a...
articles.body_html:
I wrote four security findings against a 47-line Node service. Two of them were false. One cites a file that does not exist.

Cloudflare's findings validator passed all four.

That is not a bug in the validator. It is the clearest way I found to show where the value of an AI security review actually sits.

The skill

cloudflare/security-audit-skill is a coding-agent skill that turns one agent into a coordinator of many: recon agents map the code, hunter agents look for bugs, and fresh verifier agents try to knock each finding down before it reaches a report. It was on GitHub trending this week with almost 2,000 stars in a day, 35,690 in total when I checked. MIT licensed. Cloudflare says it is the starting point of the vulnerability harness they now run across their whole fleet.

I measured it before reading it closely. The skill is 15 markdown files: 1,778 lines, 24,768 words, about 183 KB. At the usual four bytes per token that is roughly 46,000 tokens of instructions, loaded in pieces as a run needs them. Cloudflare's blog post says the first version was about 450 lines.

Two zero-dependency Node scripts sit beside the prose: validate-findings.cjs (773 lines) and validate-coverage-ledger.cjs (872 lines). Their own test suites ran clean on my machine, 34 and 31 tests.

The part that caught my eye is the proportion. Of the six phases, two exist only to disprove: Phase 3 hands every candidate to a fresh agent told to refute it, and Phase 5 sends another fresh agent over the final record (the quick profile merges the two). Each Phase 3 verifier prompt carries about 17.5 KB of fixed text before it sees the candidate: a six-step refutation prompt, a file-promotion procedure, and three schema branches copied in verbatim.

What I actually did

I did not install the skill, and no agent ran it. The README's install path is a skills CLI that writes into your agent's config, and I don't do that for a post.

Instead I wrote a small target, played the hunter by hand, and ran the skill's real validator on the result. The target is a notes service on node:http and node:sqlite with dummy users alice and bob. These are the two functions that matter:

function search(user, q) {
  const sql = "SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE owner = '" + user + "' AND title LIKE '%" + q + "%'";
  return db.prepare(sql).all();
}

function getNote(user, id) {
  return db.prepare('SELECT id, title, body FROM notes WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?').get(id, user);
}

There is also an /admin/export route gated on X-Forwarded-For starting with 10..

Then I wrote four findings the way a hunter returns them, in the skill's schema:

  1. SQL injection in search. Real.
  2. SQL injection in getNote, marked confirmed, with an observed result claiming it returned bob's note. False.
  3. SQL injection in findUser at src/users.js line 212. Invented: that file does not exist.
  4. The export gate trusts a header a client can set, unless a proxy rewrites it. A real question, but the proxy is not in the repo.

What the validator checks 

$ node validate-findings.cjs proposed.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

To be fair to it, it does enforce the contract. When I raised one record's overall severity above its impact, or put a severity on the needs_validation record, it failed, with exact paths. It checks shape, ordering, safe relative paths, and that a confirmed record has an observed result written in visible text.

It never opens a source file. It doesn't take the target path at all. The skill says this itself, in one line of Phase 4: validator success "proves format and ledger consistency only." A hunter's observed result is a string, and my invented one was schema-valid.

A cheap check gets one

Next I wrote 15 lines of Node that open every cited file and check the line exists:

ok   admin/export-xff-gate
ok   notes/note-sql-concat
ok   notes/search-sql-concat
FAIL users/find-user-template-sql  src/routes/login.js: no such file; src/users.js: no such file

That kills the invented file. Cloudflare's harness has the same idea in plain code: per the blog, deterministic code confirms the cited files and paths exist before a finding moves on.

It does nothing for the getNote claim. Line 24 is real, and it really runs a query with the id in it. Every fact the record cites is true except the one that matters.

The skeptic gets the rest

So I walked the Phase 3 prompt by hand. Step 2 says to rebuild the strongest control on the path. For getNote that takes one read: id and owner are bound as placeholders. Step 3 says to reproduce the minimum result yourself. My service is my own code with dummy data, so I ran it on loopback (the skill demands an OS-enforced sandbox before it runs anyone else's target; this was not that). Output trimmed:

search, normal     200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"}]
search, payload    200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"},{"id":2,"title":"payroll"}]
note, bob id       200 null
note, payload      200 null
note, payload 2    200 null
export, XFF 10.    200 [... both users' notes ...]

The search payload ' OR 1=1 -- hands alice the title of bob's note. Every getNote payload returns nothing. The export gate opens to a header alone, but whether a client can send that header in production depends on a proxy the repo doesn't contain, so it stays needs_validation with an owner check attached. That is the skill's rule for a deployment fact, and I agree with it.

The final file: one confirmed, one needs validation, two rejected.

$ node validate-findings.cjs findings.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

Same validator, same four fingerprints, same PASS. In between, two of the three "confirmed" bugs became rejected. Only reading the code at the cited line and running the payload told the files apart.

Why the skeptic is the expensive part

Finding candidates is cheap now. Cloudflare's blog reports 20,799 raw candidates from their discovery harness, of which about 12,057 survived validation, and an early validation rejection rate of 40% before better recon brought it down to 11%. At 40%, a team without a refuter gets four bad tickets in every ten. Somebody pays for those, and it's usually a maintainer.

That is also the theme of OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" post on coordinating disclosure as agents surface critical bugs, which was on the Hacker News front page the same day.

So my claim: when you judge an AI security tool, judge the step that tries to prove the finding wrong. The hunt is a hypothesis generator. The product is the record that survived.

Where it falls short

Cost is real. In the Hacker News thread, jesse_dot_id reported at least 150k tokens on a fairly small FastAPI project before hitting a session limit. Issue #20 is a blind test on one seeded target, three rounds per arm, by a team with its own competing tool, which it discloses. There the quick profile cost a median $29.95 against $2.06 for one plain agent, and found the same share of the seeded bugs (a median recall of 0.467 for both). On a small, clean target the skeptic may have nothing to kill.

And a skeptic that shares the hunter's model is not fully independent. Per that same issue, the skill's verifiers inherit the session's model. Cloudflare's own pipeline triages with a different model from the one that hunts. Fresh context is not a different mind.

If you run AI reviews on your code today, what does the step that tries to disprove a finding look like: a second model, a test that must fail before the fix, or you?

articles.title: A wrong "closed" never comes back: measuring a job-posting liveness checker on real pages
articles.description: What I found in career-ops's liveness checker over 16 merged PRs, how I measured each fix on real job pages, and what it taught me about permanent decisions.
articles.body_html:
career-ops is an open-source job-search pipeline: Node.js scripts driven by AI coding CLIs, with about 76k stars on GitHub. Before it adds a posting to your pipeline, scan --verify checks that the posting is still open. Where the job board has a public API, it asks the API. Otherwise it loads the page in a headless browser and reads it.

A "closed" or "blocked" verdict goes into your scan history for good, and that posting is skipped on every later scan. So the two ways to be wrong cost very different amounts. A wrong "open" costs one more check later. A wrong "closed" makes a live job disappear from your search without a trace.

Between 3 and 20 October 2026 I had 16 pull requests merged into career-ops, most of them in this liveness checker. This is what I found, how I measured it, and what the fixes look like.

How I found the bugs

The board was busy: 135 open PRs and 208 open issues on 11 October. The project's CONTRIBUTING lets bug fixes go in without an issue, so instead of competing for claimed issues I read modules nobody was working on. I started with the ATS keyword and CV skill checks, which are close to my NLP background, then moved to the liveness checker.

For the checker, I ran it on real postings and read every disagreement. The sources were public job-postings datasets (LinkedIn, USAJOBS) and live boards without an API. Several fixes also came out of the project's own conversations: a merge note from the maintainer, a follow-up the review bot offered, and three follow-ups from my reviews of other contributors' PRs.

A blocked tracker took the whole page down

Many people run a DNS filter that blocks ads and trackers: Pi-hole, AdGuard DNS, Control D, a hosts-file blocklist. Such a filter answers 0.0.0.0 for a tracker it blocks.

The browser check has a security guard that refuses requests to private network addresses, and 0.0.0.0 is on its list. Refusing the tracker is right. But the guard also marked the whole page "blocked", which scan --verify records permanently.

I found it while reviewing another contributor's PR that touches how the guard handles DNS answers. To measure it, I took 35 postings on 19 boards with no API, all live the day before, and checked each one with main's code and with the fix, behind two real filtering resolvers and with no filter as a control:

  • On main, 12 postings behind AdGuard DNS and 20 behind Control D read "blocked".
  • With the fix, none did. Behind Control D, 11 of those 20 read active with a visible Apply button.
  • With no filter, both versions agreed on 32 of 35. The 3 differences were flaky page loads, in both directions.

The fix (#5015) leaves the guard's decision alone. The request is still refused, with the same error. The guard only tags the refusal when the only private addresses in the answer are the filter's:

  if (blocked.length > 0) {
    const denied = new Error(`Access denied: Egress guard blocked private target IP ${blocked[0].ip}`);
    if (blocked.every(({ hit }) => SINKHOLE_ADDRESSES.has(hit))) denied.livenessCode = 'dns_sinkhole';
    throw denied;
  }

A tagged refusal of a tracker, a script or an image no longer decides the page's verdict. Any other private address still counts, even next to 0.0.0.0. I rejected the simpler option, ignoring every private answer for subresources, because it would drop the guard's signal on a host that really resolves into a private network.

The follow-up, #5075, covers the posting's own host. When that host had no usable address, the guard reported "blocked". But no address is often about the run, not the posting: a DNS outage during the scan, or the user's own filter blocking the job board. Now it reads uncertain, and the posting is kept for another check. With the posting's own host failing DNS, 19 of 19 postings from 19 boards were dropped permanently on main, and 19 of 19 were kept with the fix.

The PR states the trade-off: a domain that is really gone now reads uncertain too, because one failed lookup can't tell a dead domain from an outage. A kept dead posting costs one more check later. A pinned live one never comes back.

One failed load failed the rest of the run

This one turned up while I was measuring another fix: a posting whose host no longer resolved broke the checks after it in the same run. I reproduced it on the code from before my DNS change, to rule that out, and traced it to the browser library the next day.

The checker runs every browser check in one tab. When a page fails to load (its host has no address, its certificate has expired, its connection is reset), the browser shows its error page a moment after the checker has moved on, and that interrupts the next page load. The interrupted page then finishes loading late and interrupts the one after it, often to the end of the run. Those checks fail as load errors, so scan --verify keeps the postings without having checked them, and the closed ones among them go into the user's pipeline. The root is a known Playwright issue (microsoft/playwright#35944, closed upstream without a fix).

Through the real CLI, on one list of 45 URLs with 6 failing loads spread among 39 postings that were live the day before:

  • On main, 39 of 39 postings read as load errors, from the first URL to the last.
  • With the fix, none did: 30 active, 1 expired (HTTP 404), 6 "no Apply control", 1 Cloudflare challenge and 1 timeout.

Over 36 failed loads, the browser's error page landed 1 to 69 ms after the failure was reported, median 4 ms. So the fix (#5299) waits for the browser's own signal instead of a fixed delay, for at most 2 s:

async function navigateSettled(page, navigate) {
  try {
    return await navigate();
  } catch (err) {
    const canWait = typeof page.waitForEvent === 'function' && typeof page.mainFrame === 'function';
    if (canWait && err?.name !== 'TimeoutError') {
      await page
        .waitForEvent('framenavigated', {
          predicate: (frame) => frame === page.mainFrame() && frame.url().startsWith('chrome-error:'),
          timeout: FAILED_NAVIGATION_COMMIT_MS,
        })
        .catch(() => {});
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

A timeout is left alone: a timed-out load shows no error page, and the next load cancels it, so waiting would only add 2 s. I rejected parking the tab on a blank page after a failure, which another part of the code does after a search, because that load is interrupted the same way. The review bot pointed out that the old page changing its own address could end the wait too early. I couldn't make that happen in real Chromium in 26 tries, but fixed it anyway, with a test the first version fails.

CI installs no browser, so the tests use a stand-in page that plays out the browser's order of events. The same sequences also run on real Chromium where it can launch.

A ground truth showed a case the issue had missed

I filed #4832 for live postings on seven non-English boards that read as having no Apply button. getManfred, a Spanish tech-job board, was one. Its Apply button says "¡Apúntame!" ("sign me up"), which the checker didn't know, so every live posting read "no Apply control".

getManfred's own feed marks every offer open or closed, so the A/B could measure against the board instead of against my reading of pages. The first run showed a case the issue had missed: one closed posting read open on both versions. Closed postings written in English often have an FAQ button such as "Can I apply if I live outside Spain?", and the English Apply pattern took it for an Apply button.

The page does say the offer is closed, but that sentence renders near the bottom, after the checker's first look on some pages. Above the title, from the start, a closed posting says when it closed ("Oferta cerrada el 27/07/2023"). Closing patterns are read before the Apply button, so an FAQ button can't outvote the date. The fix (#5350) is two patterns:

  /\boferta cerrada el \d{1,2}\/\d{1,2}\/\d{4}/i,  // a closing pattern, read before the Apply button
  /\bapuntame\b/i,                                // an Apply label, accent-free like the others

I left out the verb "aplicar": 73 of the 111 getManfred pages I measured have an FAQ button that uses it, closed ones included. On 136 real page loads:

  • Live: all 28 open offers read active with the fix. On main, 25 read "no Apply control", and the other 3 read active only through their FAQ button.
  • Closed: all 83 read closed with the fix. On main, 17 read active, all of them written in English and read through the FAQ button.

The board already knew the answer

No Fluff Jobs, a Polish tech-job board, was the last of my board families from #4832, and the checker read it backwards. A live posting puts its Apply button ("Aplikuj") inside a page header, which the checker skips as page chrome, so every live posting read "no Apply control". A closed posting moves to a search page with a promo link that also says "Aplikuj", so most closed postings read as open.

I'd planned label patterns. Then I found that the board's per-posting API says directly whether a posting is open. So the fix (#5428) is an API rung, as several other boards already have. The API answers "published" (open), "expired" (closed) or "does not exist". A status the rung doesn't know reads uncertain, never closed, and an answer it can't read falls back to the browser.

Through the real CLI on 102 postings (40 live from the board's search API, 59 closed from Wayback Machine archives, 1 gone and 2 made up):

  • On main, all 40 live postings read "no Apply control", and 42 of the 59 closed ones read active.
  • With the fix, 40 of 40 read active and 59 of 59 read closed, without opening a browser: 26 s against 348 s.

The review bot raised two valid points on it. I measured that they change no verdict on today's API answers and shipped them as a follow-up, #5533.

VDAB, the job board of Flanders' public employment service, looks like the second case. A closed vacancy there keeps its page and its Apply button, and only a banner says it's closed. Reading the page while it renders, main read 13 of 84 loads of closed vacancies as open. My open PR, #5703, asks VDAB's per-vacancy API, which the page itself uses. One choice in it is deliberate: a "pending" vacancy reads uncertain, not closed, because one pending vacancy had never been published at all, and a closed verdict is recorded for good.

How each fix was tested

Every PR adds tests that fail on main and pass with the fix. I checked each one with mutation variants: deliberately broken versions of the fix that the tests must catch. On #4810, 13 of 13 were caught; on #4833, 12 of 12. I also ran the full suite on each branch against main. Over three weeks it grew from about 11,600 to about 16,800 tests.

Among the things the maintainer's merge notes thanked were the edge-case tests: in the keyword check, the ones that keep "IT", "HR" and "AWS" from matching ordinary words; in the checker, the one for a button that is hidden or sits in the navigation.

The rest of the work

  • Four fixes to the ATS keyword-coverage and CV skill-gap checks. The keyword check, for one, looked for a single English heading, so reports in the translated modes stopped with an error. Here is the same report under each mode's heading on main, from #4725: 
  en  ## Keywords extracted         exit 0  coverage 80%
  de  ## Extrahierte Keywords       exit 1  No "## Keywords extracted" block found (or it is empty).
  es  ## Palabras clave extraídas   exit 1  same
  ko  ## 추출한 키워드              exit 1  same
  zh  ## ATS 关键词提取             exit 1  same

On the branch, all five exit 0 at 80%.

  • One fix to the Gupy provider, whose API had moved to another host. It closed #4831, which I filed.
  • Reviews of five other contributors' liveness and scan PRs, all merged. Four authors applied my findings or suggested tests before merge, and a fifth took my suggestion into a new version.
  • #4832 is closed: every board in it has a merged fix. We split it by approach instead of racing. The contributor who wrote the providers for its Chinese boards moved them to per-posting APIs, another contributor took CareerViet, and I did the Dutch boards, getManfred and No Fluff Jobs.

Three more PRs are open: #5535 (HiringRoom's "Postularse" label, approved), #5691 (Tech in Asia's Apply link in the page header) and #5703 (VDAB's API). Since 9 October I've been on the project's contributors team. Thanks to the maintainer for quick merges and for merge notes that say exactly what they valued.

What I learned

  • Mistakes aren't symmetric when a pipeline makes permanent decisions. A false "open" costs one more check later. A false "closed" can't be undone. Most of my liveness fixes move an unsure case from permanent to retry-next-time.
  • Find a ground truth before trusting an A/B. getManfred's feed and VDAB's API measured the fixes, not my reading of pages. getManfred's feed also showed a case the issue had missed.
  • Look for the board's own API before patching the page reader. No Fluff Jobs looked like a label-and-pattern job. Its API answered both sides directly, needed no browser, and left the rules every board shares untouched.
  • Measure before changing a rule every board shares. The header skip looked like a bug on every board, but 821 real pages from 268 sites showed it hid only one board's Apply button. So #5691 (open) reads one narrow case, a link to the posting's own page, instead of every button in every header.
  • Separate the change from the page. Live pages differ from one load to the next, so two runs can disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with the code. Running both versions on the same loaded page at the same moment settles it: on #5691's control pages, all 5 verdict differences came with identical button lists.
  • Some bugs live between two systems. The failed-load chain came from the browser and its automation library disagreeing about when a failed load is over. Waiting for the browser's own signal stops the chain, at a cost of a few milliseconds per failed load.
  • Reviews count as contributions. Reviewing another contributor's DNS change led straight to the bug #5015 fixes.

All 16 merged PRs: https://github.com/career-ops-hq/career-ops/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+author%3Aroydonsequeira

articles.title: How I built Word-style A4 pages for TipTap without touching the document
articles.description: If you've built an editor with TipTap / ProseMirror, you've probably heard this request: "Make it...
articles.body_html:
If you've built an editor with TipTap / ProseMirror, you've probably heard this request: "Make it look like Word. Show real A4 pages, and print exactly what I see."

Sounds simple, but a contenteditable is one endless column of content. It has no idea what a page is.

This post walks through how I added A4 pagination to my open-source editor, Text Editor React, and packaged it as a free extension: tiptap-a4-pagination.

👉 Live demo: https://text-editor-react-neon.vercel.app/

The options I found

Option Problem
Tiptap Pages (official) Paid Pro extension, private npm registry
Community extensions Inject global CSS (change table display, word-break: break-all, force padding/width on the editor), which broke my existing styles
One editor per page Cursor movement, undo and selections across pages become a nightmare

I wanted one thing: don't modify the document, don't touch the user's CSS. editor.getHTML() should stay exactly as clean as before.

The idea: spacers as decorations

ProseMirror has decorations: elements that are rendered but are not part of the document. So:

  1. Measure every top-level block (paragraphs, headings, tables, images…).
  2. When a block would cross the bottom of a page, insert a widget decoration right before it.
  3. Make the widget exactly as tall as the rest of the page + bottom margin + the gray gap + the next page's top margin.

The block lands at the top of the next sheet, and visually you get separate pages. The document doesn't change by a single byte.

Decoration.widget(pos, () => createSpacer(pageBreak), { side: -1, ignoreSelection: true })

The layout is recomputed whenever the editor's height changes (typing, images loading, fonts arriving) with a ResizeObserver and requestAnimationFrame.

Don't trust the current positions

My first attempt used each block's getBoundingClientRect().top. The problem: the spacers I had already inserted shift those positions. Measure again, get a different answer, move the spacers, measure again… an endless loop.

What works is to rebuild the layout from heights and margins only, as if there were no spacers at all:

let cursor: number | null = null   // bottom of the previous block
let pageEnd = layout.contentHeight

for (const block of blocks) {
  // Adjacent vertical margins collapse, like in CSS
  const top = cursor === null
    ? block.top
    : cursor + Math.max(prevMarginBottom, block.marginTop)
  const bottom = top + block.height

  if (bottom > pageEnd && top > pageStart) {
    // Spacer before this block: it starts at the top of the next page
    breaks.push({ pos: block.pos, height: nextPageTop - block.marginTop - (cursor + prevMarginBottom) })
    pageEnd += pitch
  }
  cursor = bottom
}

This function is pure: blocks in, page breaks out, no DOM. That made it easy to unit test, and the package has 13 tests for this part alone.

The traps I fell into

1. Margin collapse

Once a spacer sits between two paragraphs, their margins stop collapsing, and everything is off by a few pixels. On top of that, the first block's top margin "leaks" out of the editor, which shifted my origin by 16px. The fix was to measure from the top of the page's content area (the page's padding-top), not from the editor element.

2. Floated images

An image with float: left (text wrapping) doesn't push the next block down: the next paragraph sits beside it. The layout has to skip a floated block's height when placing the following block.

3. Splitting tables across pages

Pushing a long table to the next page as a whole looks terrible. Instead, inside a table the spacer is a <tr>: a widget decoration placed between two row nodes.

The biggest bug here: I gave the spacer cell colSpan = 1000, "to be safe". With table-layout: fixed, the browser created 1000 phantom columns and squeezed the real ones to almost nothing, so text stacked one character per line. The fix: use the real column count, TableMap.get(table).width from prosemirror-tables.

4. Rowspan

Inserting a spacer row in the middle of a cell with rowspan breaks the table instantly. Rows joined by a rowspan are grouped into one unbreakable group, and page breaks only go between groups.

5. Repeating the header row

Like Word, when a table continues on the next page, its header row shows again. I copy the first row's DOM (with the measured width of each cell, so the columns line up) into the end of the spacer row.

6. Zoom

Later I added a Google Docs–style zoom (50–200%) with a CSS transform: scale() on the page. Every getBoundingClientRect() suddenly returned scaled values, and page breaks moved around with the zoom level. Now the extension divides every measurement by the page's on-screen scale:

export function elementScale (element: HTMLElement): number {
  return element.getBoundingClientRect().width / element.offsetWidth || 1
}

offsetWidth ignores transforms, so the ratio is the zoom. Page breaks are now identical at every level.

PDF export without a server

The project used to export PDFs through a Puppeteer backend. Now it prints through the browser (window.print() on a hidden iframe containing only the pages):

  • @page { size: A4; margin: ... } comes from the page settings.
  • Spacers are removed and break-before: page goes on the block right after each one, so the PDF breaks exactly where the editor does.
  • Table header rows move into a <thead>, and Chrome repeats them on every printed page.
  • Headers, footers and page numbers use CSS page margin boxes (Chrome 131+): 
@page {
  @top-left     { content: "Quarterly report"; }
  @bottom-right { content: "Page " counter(page) " of " counter(pages); }
}

Use it in your project 

npm install tiptap-a4-pagination

import { Pagination, createPageLayout } from 'tiptap-a4-pagination'
import 'tiptap-a4-pagination/styles.css'

// Margins in mm
const layout = createPageLayout({ size: 'A4', marginTop: 25.4, marginBottom: 25.4 })

const editor = useEditor({
  extensions: [StarterKit, Pagination.configure({ pageSelector: '.page' })]
})

useEffect(() => { editor?.commands.setPageLayout(layout) }, [editor])

About 5 KB gzipped, TipTap 3 only. Full docs are in the package README.

Limitations

  • A single paragraph taller than the space left on a page moves to the next page as a whole; paragraphs are not split across two pages yet.
  • A table row taller than a whole page overflows into the gap.

What else is in the editor

Comments in the margin, link sharing with real-time editing (peer-to-peer over WebRTC with Yjs, no backend), headers and footers, opening .docx files, Google Docs paste that keeps checklists and tables, slash commands, find & replace, and zoom. All MIT.

I'd love feedback, especially documents that break the layout. If you find it useful, a ⭐ on GitHub would mean a lot 🙏

  • GitHub: https://github.com/HuyPhan1232203/Text-editor-react
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/tiptap-a4-pagination
  • Demo: https://text-editor-react-neon.vercel.app/

articles.title: WebMCP in practice: testing music, CSVs, and page edits
articles.description: The model said it had written a melody and “read it back to verify.” The call log told a slightly...
articles.body_html:
The model said it had written a melody and “read it back to verify.” The call log told a slightly different story: one read, then one write. There was no second read.

The write operation returned the saved score, so the model did have the result in context. But its explanation described an extra step that never happened.

That small discrepancy is a good example of why I built WebMCP DevTools, a Chrome extension for inspecting page tools and their execution. I want to compare what an agent says with what an application actually did.

To explore that, I made an English-language workshop with three small workspaces: a music editor, an expense dataset, and an invitation-page editor. This post walks through a fresh run using the real DeepSeek API and the tools registered by those pages.

What the webpage contributes

WebMCP is a proposed web standard for exposing structured tools from webpages. A tool has a name, a description, an input schema, and an implementation supplied by the page.

In this workshop, the useful state already exists in the browser: the current score, the current query, and the current invitation revision. A tool reads or modifies that state. The interface then renders the result, and a person can keep working on it.

The site needs to implement these capabilities. An extension cannot manufacture a reliable business API for every page you visit. Browser support is still evolving, too.

1. A melody you can keep editing

Here is the request I used:

Write an original eight-bar birthday-style melody in C major, 3/4, 108 BPM, with piano and a soft bass part. Title it A Little Birthday Waltz. Use varied note lengths and end on C.

The model called music_get_state, then music_set_song. It produced 29 piano notes and eight bass notes: 37 notes across 24 beats, about 13.33 seconds.

Each note has a pitch, start time, duration, and velocity. That makes the result editable data. I can change the bass volume while the piece is playing, modify the score, or export a MIDI file for another application.

This is symbolic music composition. There is no audio model generating a finished recording. The browser synthesizes the score, and the model is responsible for choosing the notes.

The test checked that playback entered its playing state, that the position advanced after a volume change, and that MIDI export produced a file with the expected header. It did not evaluate whether the music sounds good. The exported MIDI is available if you want to listen.

About that “read-back” claim: the saved score came back in the write response. A separate test read later confirmed it. Keeping the trace made that distinction visible.

2. A total with evidence behind it

The expense sample has nine records, including one missing amount. I asked for October spending by category, excluding missing amounts rather than treating them as zero.

The model read the dataset and called data_query with this input:

{
  "aggregate": "sum",
  "groupBy": "Category",
  "metric": "Amount",
  "filters": [
    { "column": "Date", "op": "contains", "value": "2026-10" }
  ]
}

The page calculated $275 from six usable records. Seven records matched October; one was excluded because its amount was missing.

Food accounted for $168: $48 on physical CSV row 4 and $120 on row 6. The pending food receipt on row 10 was excluded. Row 1 is the header.

That is a useful division of work. The model chooses the query and explains the result. The application computes it and returns the source rows. If I disagree with the explanation, I can inspect the data rather than rerun a conversation and hope for a better answer.

3. A page edit with a revision check

For the website example, I asked for Alex's Birthday Picnic, on October 31, 2026 at 2 PM in Riverside Park, with a warm orange accent.

This time the model made three calls: site_get_state, site_update, and another site_get_state. The invitation moved from revision 1 to revision 2.

The update requires expectedRevision. If someone changes the page after the agent reads it, a stale update is rejected. The agent must read the current state before trying again.

This is a small safeguard, but it matters when a person and an agent share an editor. A valid JSON object can still be based on outdated assumptions.

The test automation also filled the preview's RSVP form with “Sam” and two guests, checked its confirmation, and exported the HTML. Those actions were performed by the test automation, not by DeepSeek. The form is a local demonstration; it does not submit registrations to a server or send invitations.

Where the extension fits

You can install WebMCP DevTools from the Chrome Web Store. Open its side panel on a WebMCP-enabled page to inspect the available tools and run them with your own inputs.

While building these examples, I wanted a place to inspect tool descriptions and schemas, execute known inputs, and review results and errors. Those are the core jobs of WebMCP DevTools. It also provides an AI panel for connecting a model provider.

My debugging order is to test a tool with known arguments first, then let a model choose the calls. That separates an application bug from a poor tool description, an invalid argument, or an incorrect explanation.

The extension and the workshop are separate projects. The workshop supplies the application state and tool implementations; a client discovers and invokes them. The same tools can be exercised by other compatible clients.

For this English run, a small test harness connected DeepSeek to the browser's native WebMCP tools through browser automation. It did not run inside the extension's chat panel. The screenshots show actual page states; after a UI fix, recorded model arguments were replayed to capture the final interface. They are not mock conversations or translated screenshots.

What this run establishes

There were seven model-issued tool calls across the three tasks: two for music, two for data, and three for the website. All seven returned successfully. Separate checks covered playback, volume changes, exports, the RSVP form, and overflow at mobile width. The project test suite passed 27 tests, including stale-write rejection and preserving the old score after an invalid edit.

This is a small functional test, not a benchmark. The model's extra “read-back” claim is a reminder that a successful tool response and an accurate explanation are different things.

The design idea I want to keep exploring is straightforward: let the page own its validation and state, give the agent well-defined operations, and leave the result somewhere a person can inspect and continue editing.

Try it yourself

  1. Install WebMCP DevTools from the Chrome Web Store.
  2. Open the English workshop in a compatible Chrome setup.
  3. Click the extension icon to open the side panel, inspect a tool's schema, and run it with known arguments before trying a model-driven workflow.

You can use the workshop's manual controls without a model account. Native tool access requires a compatible browser setup; Chrome's documentation explains the current requirements. AI clients use your own provider credentials, and prompts, tool definitions, and returned data go to that provider. The workshop itself does not ask for an API key. Export your work before reloading the tab.

For implementation context, the extension source is WebMCP DevTools on GitHub. The English workshop is a focused companion demo, not a translation of every page in the larger Playground.

If you are adding tools to an existing application, I would be interested in how you handle edits based on stale state. Do you reject them, merge them, or ask the user to review a proposal?

Disclosure: AI assisted with implementation, testing, and drafting this article. The examples use real DeepSeek API responses and recorded browser tool executions. The seven-call count refers only to the new English run.

articles.title: I fired 20 simultaneous bookings at a typical booking app. All 20 got the slot.
articles.description: The app you built in an afternoon   Ask Claude Code, Cursor or Lovable for a booking app for...
articles.body_html:
The app you built in an afternoon

Ask Claude Code, Cursor or Lovable for a booking app for a barbershop and you'll have one by teatime. Services, staff, a calendar, Stripe checkout. It looks done, and every test you write for it passes.

Then on a Saturday morning two customers pick 10:00 with the same barber, a second apart. Both get a confirmation email. One of them turns up to find someone already in the chair.

This isn't a bad model or a lazy prompt. It's the same bug in almost every booking app that gets generated or written quickly, and tests that send one request at a time can't see it. Here's what it looks like, a test that catches it, and what fixing it properly involves.

The check every generated scheduler writes

Under the calendar there's nearly always an appointments table and a check for overlaps before each insert. With Prisma it looks like this:

async function book(staffId, start, end) {
  const clash = await prisma.appointment.findFirst({
    where: { staffId, start: { lt: end }, end: { gt: start } },
  })
  if (clash) throw new Error('Slot taken')
  return prisma.appointment.create({ data: { staffId, start, end } })
}

The overlap condition is right: two ranges overlap when each starts before the other ends. Reviewers nod it through. The problem isn't the condition, it's that checking and inserting are two separate steps.

Two customers, one slot

When two requests arrive close together, both run findFirst before either runs create. Both see an empty slot, so both insert.

Customer A                       Customer B
findFirst: no clash
                                 findFirst: no clash
create: booked
                                 create: booked   <- two bookings, one chair

It doesn't take much traffic. A popular barber on a Saturday, a class that just opened, or one customer double-tapping the button on a slow phone will do it.

The fix has to make the database refuse the second booking, not the application. In Postgres the cleanest way is an exclusion constraint, which rejects any row whose time range overlaps another for the same staff member:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

ALTER TABLE appointment
  ADD CONSTRAINT appointment_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (
    staff_id WITH =,
    tstzrange(start_at, end_at) WITH &&
  );

Now the second insert fails with error 23P01 (exclusion violation), however close together the requests are. Catch it and tell the customer the slot has just gone.

One catch if you use Prisma: its default DateTime column is timestamp without a time zone, and Postgres refuses tstzrange on it ("functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE"). Declare the columns @db.Timestamptz(3), which is what appointment times should be anyway, or use tsrange.

The constraint only covers one table and one rule. Once a booking needs a staff member and a room, or bookings can be cancelled and should free their time, you need to filter the constraint on status and lock rows in a consistent order inside a transaction, or two bookings for two resources start deadlocking each other.

The customer who is still paying

Between picking a time and finishing checkout, a customer might take two minutes or twenty. Generated apps usually do one of two things here, and both go wrong.

  • Book after payment. Someone else books the slot while the first customer is typing their card number. They pay for a time they no longer have.
  • Book before payment. The slot is taken for good, even when the customer closes the tab. Abandoned checkouts quietly fill the diary.

What works is a hold: a booking marked pending, with an expiry time, that counts as taken until it either lapses or is confirmed. That brings three rules with it.

  1. Availability treats an unexpired hold as taken and an expired one as free, at the moment you ask, without waiting for a cleanup job.
  2. Confirming re-checks the expiry under the same lock as booking. A payment that lands a second after the hold lapsed must not confirm a slot someone else now has.
  3. Something releases lapsed holds and tells the rest of your app, so a waiting customer can be offered the time.

Clock changes

A recurring booking is where this shows first. "Every Tuesday at 9:00" sounds like one time, but it's two different UTC times either side of the clocks changing. The usual generated code adds a week in milliseconds:

const WEEK = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000
const first = new Date('2026-10-20T09:00:00+01:00') // 9:00 in London, summer time
const next = new Date(first.getTime() + WEEK)
// 2026-10-27T08:00:00.000Z: 8:00 in London. The clocks went back on the 25th.

The customer's standing appointment has moved an hour and nobody touched it. The fix is to store the rule in local time with its timezone ("Tuesdays, 09:00, Europe/London") and work out each date's UTC time from that, not from the one before.

The edges matter too. When the clocks go back, 01:30 happens twice; when they go forward, 01:30 doesn't happen at all. A shop with a site in Madrid and one in London needs each site's hours in its own zone. None of this turns up in tests unless a test runs across a clock change.

Buffers and services that need two things

The overlap check assumes one booking uses one person for its whole length. Real services don't.

  • Buffers. A 45-minute cut with 10 minutes of cleanup blocks the chair for 55, but the customer should still see 45. The overlap check has to use the padded time while the confirmation shows the real one.
  • Two resources. A massage needs a therapist and a room. Both have to be free, and both have to be taken in one step, or a second booking grabs the room between the two inserts.
  • Gaps in the middle. A colour needs the stylist for 30 minutes, then not for 30 while it develops, then again. The stylist is free to take someone else in the gap.
  • "Anyone available". Picking the first free barber is another check-then-insert. Two customers asking for anyone can both be given Sam.

Each of these is fixable. Together they turn a table and a check into a scheduling engine.

A test that catches it

The fix starts with a test that fails. Fire 20 bookings for the same slot at once and count how many succeed. The answer should be one.

import { test } from 'node:test'
import assert from 'node:assert/strict'
import { book } from './booking.js'

test('one of 20 simultaneous bookings for a slot succeeds', async () => {
  const start = new Date('2026-11-14T10:00:00Z')
  const end = new Date('2026-11-14T10:45:00Z')

  const results = await Promise.allSettled(
    Array.from({ length: 20 }, () => book('staff_1', start, end)),
  )

  const booked = results.filter((r) => r.status === 'fulfilled').length
  assert.equal(booked, 1)
})

Here's what it did with the Prisma code above, 20 runs of 20 bookings each:

Setup Bookings that succeeded, per run of 20 Runs that double-booked
Check-then-insert, Postgres, pool of 20 connections 20 (1 on the first run) 19 of 20
Check-then-insert, Postgres, pool of 1 connection 20 20 of 20
Check-then-insert, SQLite 19 or 20 20 of 20
With the exclusion constraint 1 0 of 20

Two things surprised me. The first run passed, because the pool was still opening connections one at a time, which spaced the requests out. So run it more than once.

And neither a single connection nor SQLite saves you. All 20 reads run before any of the 20 writes, however the queries queue, so every one of them sees an empty slot.

Add a second test that holds a slot, moves time past its expiry, and checks that the confirm is refused. Then one that books a weekly series across the last Sunday in October and checks every date stays at 9:00 local.

Build it, or hand it off

You don't always need any of this. A table and a check are fine when:

  • one person takes bookings for themselves and can sort out the odd clash by phone,
  • there's no payment between picking a time and booking it, and
  • everything happens in one timezone, with no recurring bookings, buffers or shared rooms.

If you're building for many businesses, each with staff, rooms and customers paying online, the scheduling is a product of its own. You can build it: an exclusion constraint, holds with expiry, rules in local time, locks taken in a fixed order, and tests for each. Or you can hand it to a service built for it.

That's why we built Tiempo, a scheduling API for booking platforms. Your app keeps its services, prices, customers and payments; Tiempo keeps the time. Every booking locks the resources it touches, so the race above ends in one booking and one 409. Holds expire on their own, recurring bookings keep their local time through clock changes, and buffers, two-resource services and "anyone available" are built in. It has a free test mode, and a rules file you can give your coding agent so it uses Tiempo instead of writing a scheduler.

To see all of it in one place, the booking starter is a small Next.js barbershop app on Tiempo: pick a service, a barber or anyone, and a time, and the slot is held while you pay, with Stripe or a built-in test page. A payment that lands after its hold ran out is refunded, not forced through. It ships with the race test from above, aimed at the real thing:

20 customers racing for 2026-10-23T08:15:00Z...
Held: 1. Refused with 409: 19. Other errors: 0.
Pass: one booking, no double-booking.

It's MIT-licensed, and its AGENTS.md tells your coding agent how it uses Tiempo, so you can fork it and ask the agent to turn it into your product.

Whichever way you go, write the race test first. It's ten lines, and it tells you whether your booking app can be trusted on a busy Saturday.
